Top half is a photo we took on the recce. Bottom half is what ended up in the edit.

We shot the whole location on our phones a few weeks before the shoot. Framing, lens, where the lamp stands, where the actor sits. Then we tick it off one by one on the day.

It's a bit much, sure. But it means nobody is standing in a living room at 8am wondering where to put the camera. By the time the crew walks in, most of it is already decided.

No crew flew to the Alps for this one.

We made a spec commercial for G-Star. Fully AI generated. Not because we think AI should replace a film set, but because we want to know exactly what it can do before a client asks us.

So we treated it like any other job. A concept first. Then a treatment. Then a look: cold blue light, snow moving over a ridge, one man on top of a mountain at the end of the day. We storyboarded it. We picked the frames. We graded it. We did the sound.

The tools changed. The process did not.

What we learned is simple. AI is fast at giving you images. It is slow at giving you the right one. The work is still in the choosing. Which frame lands, which one is just pretty, where the cut goes, how long you stay on a face before you let it go.

That close up of the eyes is the whole film for us. Snow in the lashes, nothing else happening. You can get there with a camera. You can get there with a prompt. Either way somebody has to decide that this is the shot.

We keep making these because we would rather find the limits ourselves than read about them. Some things still do not work. 

This is spec work. Not made for G-Star, not commissioned by anyone. Just us testing a pipeline on a brand we like.

The full video is on our site. Link in bio.

If you are a brand or an agency thinking about where AI fits in your next campaign, come talk to us. We will tell you honestly what it can carry and what it cannot.

Nobody expects a padel app to save a friend group. This one did.

There is a group in Amsterdam that had not been together in one room since the summer. Not because anything happened. Nothing happened at all, and that was exactly the problem.

It always went the same way. Someone suggested padel. Four people said yes. Then the group chat spent three days hunting for an evening that worked, and by the time it found one, two of them had booked something else.

So they stopped asking. Not on purpose. The messages just got further apart, and then they stopped coming.

In October one of them tried something different. Instead of planning one evening, they set up a whole season: a CASUAL COMPETITION, the EffePadelle format that runs for weeks or months. Everyone plays everyone once, at their own pace, and there is no end date to miss.

One link went into the group chat. Eight people made an account and they were in.

From there the app took over the boring part.

It builds every round itself, so nobody has to work out who plays who. That one question has quietly ended more padel groups than any argument ever has.

Everyone linked their calendar once, and the app showed the evenings nobody was busy. Green means everybody can play. Rather not share your calendar? Tap your availability in by hand and it works exactly the same.

After a match you type in the three sets. Your opponent taps to confirm. The table updates itself, and the standings sit there in the open all season, which is usually what gets people to show up.

They have played every week since. The group chat is busier than it has been in two years, and the standings are, by all accounts, a problem.

Both formats are free. A CASUAL COMPETITION runs for months. A ONE DAY TOURNAMENT is finished in an afternoon. Plenty of groups run both.

Send this to the group chat that went quiet. That is the whole point.

Search EffePadelle in the App Store or on Google Play.
